meta.title: Effectiveness of agricultural interventions that aim to improve nutritional status of children: systematic review
meta.organisation: Institute of Development Studies, University of Sussex
meta.country: Multiple low and middle income countries

brief.intended_change: Improve children's nutritional status and reduce under-nutrition.
brief.population: Children in low and middle income countries, particularly children aged under 5 in households targeted by agricultural programmes.
brief.time_horizon: Varies by programme; no common intervention duration or follow-up period is specified.
brief.intervention: Food-based agricultural programmes explicitly intended to improve child nutrition, including home gardens, bio-fortified crops, aquaculture and small scale fisheries, dairy development, animal husbandry, and poultry development. Dosage varies and is not specified consistently.
brief.context: The review covers 23 studies published after 1990, predominantly evaluations of home gardens. These are complex interventions implemented in settings where poverty and the health environment can affect nutritional outcomes.
brief.outcome_first: Develop a theory of change for improving children's nutritional status and reducing under-nutrition in low and middle income countries. Focus particularly on children under 5 in poor households.
brief.intervention_first: Develop a theory of change for food-based agricultural programmes explicitly intended to improve children's nutritional status in low and middle income countries. These programmes include home gardens, bio-fortified crops, fisheries, aquaculture, and livestock development.

verdict.raw: No study reported participation rates or the programme’s ability to reach the targeted population. No study described the socioeconomic characteristics of participants or the determinants of participation.
The interventions were successful in promoting the consumption of food rich in protein and micronutrients, but the effect on the overall diet of poor people remains unclear.
verdict.quote: the effect on the overall diet of poor people remains unclear

verdict.raw: Five studies reported a large positive effect of the interventions on total household income. However, only in one case was the difference between project and control groups statistically tested.
verdict.quote: the overall effect on household income remains unclear

verdict.raw: No evidence was found of an effect on the absorption of iron, but some evidence exists of a positive effect on absorption of vitamin A.
verdict.quote: some evidence exists of a positive effect on absorption of vitamin A

verdict.raw: Overall, these results provide little support for the hypothesis that agricultural interventions help to reduce under-nutrition. However, they should not be interpreted as evidence of the absence of an effect.
verdict.quote: they should not be interpreted as evidence of the absence of an effect

assumptions.text: Not all targeted populations are able to join programmes, and the interventions can miss vulnerable groups.

verdict.raw: we cannot tell how well targeted these programmes were, whether vulnerable groups were effectively reached, or what the effect was on specific subgroups.
verdict.quote: we cannot tell how well targeted these programmes were

assumptions.text: As income from one source increases, income from another source may decrease if households shift, for example, labour supply from farming to home gardens.
An increase in the consumption of the food item targeted by the intervention does not imply an improvement in the overall diet, because substitution effects in consumption occur.

verdict.raw: Bushamuka et al found that although the consumption of vegetables, rice, and fish increased after the intervention, the consumption of pulses decreased.

assumptions.text: Parents’ caring practices and health status can affect children’s nutritional status; the health environment and cultural practices can interfere with implementation at each stage.

verdict.raw: an intervention successfully increased the consumption of food rich in vitamin A among children, but a parasitic infestation in the intervention areas reduced the observed values of serum retinol.
verdict.quote: a parasitic infestation in the intervention areas reduced the observed values of serum retinol

context: Under-nutrition is a complex phenomenon determined by multiple causes.
Most included studies evaluated home gardens; rigorous evaluations of dairy development, animal husbandry, and fisheries projects were extremely rare.
Few bio-fortification programmes had operated long enough to be rigorously evaluated.
Study designs, outcome metrics, and follow-up periods varied substantially.

key_claims.claim: Targeted households must be able to participate before they can adopt the promoted technologies.

verdict.raw: No study reported participation rates or the programme’s ability to reach the targeted population. No study described the socioeconomic characteristics of participants or the determinants of participation.

key_claims.claim: Agricultural programmes increase production of the foods they promote.
key_claims.where: Results; Discussion; What this study adds

verdict.raw: The interventions reviewed had a positive effect on the production of agricultural goods promoted
verdict.quote: a positive effect on the production of agricultural goods promoted

key_claims.claim: Adopting the promoted agricultural activities raises total household income, rather than merely replacing other income sources.

verdict.raw: Some studies reported a positive effect on incomes from a particular source, such as income from home gardens. This measure of effect is imprecise, because substitution effects in production are possible. As a result, the overall effect on household income remains unclear.
verdict.quote: the overall effect on household income remains unclear

key_claims.claim: Promoting agricultural foods increases their consumption, but improving the whole diet also requires avoiding adverse substitution.

verdict.raw: Of the 23 studies selected, 19 reported a positive effect on the composition of the diet. With very few exceptions, home garden programmes increased the consumption of fruit and vegetables, aquaculture and small fisheries interventions increased the consumption of fish, and dairy development projects increased the consumption of milk. An increase in the consumption of the food item targeted by the intervention does not imply an improvement in the overall diet, because substitution effects in consumption occur.
verdict.quote: does not imply an improvement in the overall diet

key_claims.claim: Higher household income improves nutrient intake through food expenditure.
Changes in food consumption improve children's iron intake and absorption.

verdict.raw: Two studies assessed the effect on iron intake of children and found no statistically significant differences in the average haemoglobin concentrations between children in the project and control groups. Another study assessed the effect of fish consumption on iron intake at the household level and found a modest effect by using food to micronutrients conversion tables. The observed effect would have been even smaller after consideration of the actual body absorption of the iron ingested.
verdict.quote: No evidence was found of an effect on the absorption of iron

key_claims.claim: Agricultural food interventions can improve vitamin A intake and status in children under 5.

verdict.raw: Overall, the effect of the interventions is a difference of 2.4 µg/dL in serum retinol between project and control areas (z test of significance 6.35; P<0.001). This meta-analysis provides some support to the hypothesis that agricultural home gardens interventions improve vitamin A intake among children under the age of 5.
verdict.quote: provides some support to the hypothesis

key_claims.claim: Better food and nutrient intake reduces child under-nutrition.

verdict.raw: Only one study found a statistically significant effect on prevalence of stunting, whereas three studies found a positive effect on prevalence of underweight and two found a positive effect on wasting. The study by Gunaratna et al, which used rates of growth in height and weight, rather than prevalence, found a positive and statistically significant effect on nutrition. Overall, these results provide little support for the hypothesis that agricultural interventions help to reduce under-nutrition. However, they should not be interpreted as evidence of the absence of an effect.

key_claims.claim: Health conditions and caring practices can interrupt the pathway from improved diets to improved nutritional status.
key_claims.where: Introduction; Discussion—Comparison with earlier reviews and limitations

verdict.raw: an intervention successfully increased the consumption of food rich in vitamin A among children, but a parasitic infestation in the intervention areas reduced the observed values of serum retinol.
verdict.quote: a parasitic infestation in the intervention areas reduced the observed values of serum retinol

key_claims.claim: A lack of statistically significant nutritional effects does not establish that the agricultural pathway is ineffective.

verdict.raw: On average, the probability of detecting a small effect for these studies was less than 5%. Even a “large” effect (that is, a reduction in malnutrition by 30%) would be detected in only 50% of cases. A more realistic medium effect of 10% would be detected with a probability of only 15%. The lack of power of the studies reviewed could have prevented the identification of any effect.
verdict.quote: the lack of power of the studies reviewed could have prevented the identification of any effect

overall.raw: The question posed by the review cannot be answered with any level of confidence. The data available show a poor effect of these interventions on nutritional status, but methodological weaknesses of the studies cast serious doubts on the validity of these results.
overall.quote: cannot be answered with any level of confidence

conclusions.summary: The interventions increased production and consumption of promoted foods, and some evidence supports improved vitamin A intake. Their effects on total household income and overall diet remain unclear, and no evidence of improved iron absorption was found. Very little evidence supports reductions in stunting, wasting, or underweight, but low statistical power and other methodological weaknesses prevent interpreting this as evidence of ineffectiveness. Participation, targeting, and subgroup effects were not adequately documented. The review cannot guide prioritisation among competing interventions without cost-effectiveness evidence.
recommendations: Use credible counterfactual methods; use matched longitudinal or cross sectional project-control studies when randomisation is infeasible.
Avoid before/after comparisons and participant/non-participant comparisons that do not control for selection bias.
Investigate why poor people participate or do not participate, including whether vulnerable groups are reached.
Use total household income, consumption, and dietary diversity measures rather than only income or consumption of the promoted product.
Collect anthropometric measurements with sufficiently large samples and always conduct power calculations.
Consider rigorous evaluations of intermediate outcomes and efficacy within the complex causal chain.
Establish agreed standards and guidelines for rigorous evaluation.
Exercise caution about expected nutritional effects and develop cost-effectiveness evidence.
